topic.title: The kirana runs a credit bureau
topic.claim: The corner shop that lets you pay at month-end trusts you on data no bank has, and that's genuinely good.
topic.moment: You're short on cash, the shopkeeper says 'baad mein de dena', and writes it in a diary.

turn.believed: Udhaar is just an old, informal habit that's dying out.
turn.actually: It's a credit system that reads your character off years of showing up, which an app can't do.

topic.because: He knows your routine, your family, whether you keep your word. That lived knowledge beats a credit score built on documents you don't fully control.
topic.payoff: The shop that extends you credit on a handshake is backing you harder than any bank app ever will.
topic.behaviour: Neighbourhood shops extend informal credit based on long personal knowledge.
topic.mechanism: Years of observed behaviour beat a document-based score for judging trust.
topic.group: anyone who still shops at a local kirana
topic.send_to: the friend who's gone fully cashless and app-only
topic.why_now: quick-commerce is quietly replacing the shop that actually knew you

score.why: Gives the page its genuinely-good register: the shopkeeper's udhaar diary beating an app's credit score is a warm turn, not just a rant.

topic.villain: a credit-scoring system built on paperwork instead of years of showing up

mechanism.broken_premise: None. Premise 1 is true: Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart do promise delivery in about ten minutes. Premise 2 also matches the research on store credit. One line on slide 7, 'Try saying baad mein de dena to a ten-minute delivery app,' goes too far, because those apps do offer pay-later at checkout. Blinkit has LazyPay and Simpl, and Zepto has Amazon Pay Later, LazyPay, Simpl and its own Zepto Postpaid. But that credit only reaches you after a third-party lender's approve-or-decline check. That is exactly what the next line, 'An app can approve you or decline you,' says, so the argument still stands.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Kirana udhaar is a deferred-payment tab that the owner decides on himself. He goes on what he knows about the customer, how much they spend and how they live, and pays for it with the repeat visits and loyalty it brings. Research on Indian store credit finds the borrowers are about 12% of customers but bring in over 30% of revenue, and 78% of them shop only at that store. That research also finds owners favour higher-income customers and big spenders, as well as people from their own religion or caste, so 'trust' here includes bias as well as what the owner has seen of you. Pay-later at app checkout is credit from a regulated lender or NBFC, decided by a credit bureau score and transaction data. The decision is approve or decline, the limit is set by an algorithm, and late payment brings fees and a mark on your credit record, not an awkward nod on the street.

Informal shop credit (udhaar) is typical.correct: Udhaar (shop credit) is widely documented as paperwork-free: shopkeepers track it in a handwritten khata/notebook, not a signed contract, with no collateral or formal documentation.

sources.quote: No credit scores. No collateral. No paperwork. Just a shopkeeper's quick judgment call, about whether to let a customer walk out with goods and pay later.
The khata is not a legally binding document. There are no signed contracts or collateral.

Informal shop credit (udhaar) is typical.correct: Udhaar extended by shopkeepers to regular customers is typically interest-free, settled at month-end/income timing, distinct from wholesale/trade credit between businesses which can carry interest.

sources.quote: There is zero interest charged. The credit is extended as a service, a gesture of goodwill to a loyal customer.
Around 30 percent of households borrowing from informal sources paid no interest at all, primarily because they borrowed from relatives, friends or known local lenders/traders.

Shopkeepers decide to extend credit base.correct: Academic field research (transaction data from 26 Mumbai grocery stores plus experiments with store owners) confirms shopkeepers decide on credit using direct, personal knowledge of a customer built over time — not a formal check.

sources.publisher: Wheeler Institute, London Business School (summarizing Sungu, Alhorr & Srivastava, SSRN working paper)
sources.quote: the shopkeeper often understood the household budget better than a spreadsheet ever could... decisions stem from direct experience and relationship-building with customers.
The kirana store did not need to know your credit score. It knew you.

Shopkeepers track whether a customer has.correct: Repayment history is confirmed as a live input: a field experiment found a single repaid loan materially changed a shopkeeper's willingness to extend future credit, and industry guidance lists past payment history as a standard factor in setting customer credit limits.

sources.quote: A single positive transaction—where a customer repaid a subsidized loan—dramatically shifted store owners' willingness to extend future credit.
Retailers consider factors such as previous payment history, purchase frequency, average monthly purchases, existing outstanding balance, and payment delays when setting customer credit limits.

Banks assess creditworthiness using docu.correct: Banks assess loan eligibility from documents the applicant submits (salary certificate, Form 16/ITR, bank statements, KYC proofs) — a document-based, applicant-submitted process, confirmed by a bank's own published checklist.

sources.publisher: Punjab National Bank (bank's own loan document checklist)
sources.quote: Latest Salary certificate issued by the employer (indicating gross and net salary). Income tax Return/Form16 for last 2 years whichever is applicable. Bank Statement of salary accounts for last 6/12 months whichever is applicable.
As per RBI's KYC guidelines, banks are required to collect proof of identity and officially valid documents as proof of address from customers.

Ten-minute delivery/banking apps assess.correct: Fast/instant lending and quick-commerce-adjacent credit apps (e.g., KreditBee) assess users on far more than card or payment data: personal, employment and income information, PAN/Aadhaar, bank statements, and KYC documents — and, before RBI's 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines curbed it, also device data such as contacts, call logs, files/media, camera and location. RBI's own guidelines exist precisely because these apps were pulling extensive personal data beyond payment/card data, not relying on it alone.

payment history makes up 35% of your score and is a major factor in its calculation... a lender's number one priority is your past record of paying back (or not) your loans

Your payment history is one of the factors that lenders consider when determining your creditworthiness. It shows how consistently you have made your payments on time and in full. Late payments, missed payments and delinquencies can negatively impact your CIBIL Score.

DPD, or Days Past Due, shows how many days a payment on a loan or credit card was late during a reported month... DPD is different from the amount overdue. The amount overdue tells you how much remains unpaid, while DPD tells you how late the payment was.
DPD indicates the days a payment has been delayed for... DPD essentially shows how many days the borrower has skipped or been late with payments.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Your kirana's udhaar diary trusts you more than [any bank app]
It runs on years of you showing up, not paperwork.
 

[slide 1] Your kirana's udhaar diary trusts you more than any bank app.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's the last week of the month. You're at the counter with milk, eggs and a packet of Maggi, and the UPI payment fails.

[slide 3] The tubelight hums. You start patting every pocket. He doesn't even look up. "Baad mein de dena."
He pulls out a fat diary with a rubber band around it and writes your flat number in blue ink.

[slide 4] It feels like a habit a ten-minute app will finish off. A lot of your groceries already come from one.
That app has no idea you switched from full cream to toned last year. He does.

[slide 5] A bank would want salary slips and a score built from papers you never fully see. He asked for nothing.
He has watched you walk in at 7am for years, in chappals. He knows your parents' usual order. He knows you paid on the first last time.
He's reading years of you, not a page of documents.

[slide 6] And he can afford it. Your flat is fifty steps away, and you'll be back tomorrow for bread.
Skipping a few hundred rupees would cost you the shop and an awkward nod on your own street. The rubber band snaps back on the diary. That's his entire collections department.

[slide 7] Try saying "baad mein de dena" to a ten-minute delivery app.
An app can approve you or decline you. Only he can wait for you.

[end card] Read it again the next time a delivery app is ten minutes faster than the shop down the road.
Send to the friend who's gone fully cashless and app-only and hasn't been inside a kirana in a year.

[caption] The most generous lender in your life keeps his books in a diary with a rubber band around it.

[alt text] A seven-slide carousel about the neighbourhood kirana shop that lets you pay later. The reader's UPI payment fails, the shopkeeper says 'baad mein de dena' and writes their flat number in a diary. It argues that this informal credit is not a dying habit but trust built from years of watching your routine, knowing your family and seeing you keep your word, which a bank's document-based score cannot see. He can afford it because you live nearby and will be back tomorrow. It ends by pointing out that an app can only approve or decline you, while the shopkeeper can wait for you.

9145f138bbc18b956673e912ae47141f51de75fb.broken_premise: None. Premise 1 is true: Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart do promise delivery in about ten minutes. Premise 2 also matches the research on store credit. One line on slide 7, 'Try saying baad mein de dena to a ten-minute delivery app,' goes too far, because those apps do offer pay-later at checkout. Blinkit has LazyPay and Simpl, and Zepto has Amazon Pay Later, LazyPay, Simpl and its own Zepto Postpaid. But that credit only reaches you after a third-party lender's approve-or-decline check. That is exactly what the next line, 'An app can approve you or decline you,' says, so the argument still stands.
9145f138bbc18b956673e912ae47141f51de75fb.actual_mechanism: Kirana udhaar is a deferred-payment tab that the owner decides on himself. He goes on what he knows about the customer, how much they spend and how they live, and pays for it with the repeat visits and loyalty it brings. Research on Indian store credit finds the borrowers are about 12% of customers but bring in over 30% of revenue, and 78% of them shop only at that store. That research also finds owners favour higher-income customers and big spenders, as well as people from their own religion or caste, so 'trust' here includes bias as well as what the owner has seen of you. Pay-later at app checkout is credit from a regulated lender or NBFC, decided by a credit bureau score and transaction data. The decision is approve or decline, the limit is set by an algorithm, and late payment brings fees and a mark on your credit record, not an awkward nod on the street.

cover.headline: Your kirana's udhaar diary trusts you more than [any delivery app]
cover.sub: It runs on years of you showing up, not paperwork.

paragraphs: Your kirana's udhaar diary trusts you more than any delivery app.
slides.why_swipe: Why would a shop trust me more than an app?

paragraphs: It's the last week of the month. You're at the counter with milk, eggs and a packet of Maggi, and the UPI payment fails.
The tubelight hums. You start patting every pocket. He doesn't even look up. "Baad mein de dena."
He pulls out a fat diary with a rubber band around it. The pages are soft and smell of agarbatti, and he writes your flat number in blue ink.
slides.why_swipe: Isn't this just an old habit that's on its way out?

paragraphs: It feels like a habit the quick-delivery apps will finish off. A lot of your groceries already come from one.
But he has your packet of toned milk out before you reach the counter. He knows which bread you take.
slides.why_swipe: So what does he know that the app doesn't?

paragraphs: The app on your phone sees your orders and a saved card. It never sees you walk in at 7am in chappals, year after year.
He has. He knows your parents' usual order, and that his diary has never had to chase you.
**He's reading years of you, not a page of documents.**
slides.why_swipe: But why is he willing to take the risk?

paragraphs: And he can afford it. Your flat is fifty steps away, and you'll be back tomorrow for bread.
Skipping a few hundred rupees would cost you the shop and an awkward nod on your own street. The rubber band snaps back on the diary. That's his entire collections department.
slides.why_swipe: So what happens when you come back to pay?

paragraphs: So the first of the month comes. You hand him the cash, and he finds your flat number without asking.
One blue line through it, and he's already reaching for your bread.
**He backed you on a handshake. An app has never once waited for you.**

end.save: Read it again the next time a delivery app beats the shop down the road by a few minutes.
end.send: Send to the friend who's gone fully cashless and app-only and hasn't been inside a kirana in a year.
end.promise: How money and trust really work here.

The reader's UPI payment fails, the shopkeeper says 'baad mein de dena' and writes their flat number in a diary that smells of agarbatti. It argues that this informal credit is not a dying habit that delivery apps will finish off, but trust built from years of watching your routine: he has your milk ready, knows your bread and your parents' usual order. The app sees only orders and a saved card. He can afford the risk because you live nearby and will be back tomorrow. On the first of the month you pay, he strikes a blue line through your name and reaches for your bread. It ends by saying he backed you on a handshake, and an app has never once waited for you.
